slides.heading: Welcome: Ethics & Professional Conduct
bullets: Why ethics matters in ABA
Boundaries, dual relationships and social media
Scope of competence, documentation and billing
Conduct, reporting concerns and consequences
slides.narration: Welcome to Workplace Ethics and Professional Conduct at Spectrum Squad. Whether you are a brand new R B T, an experienced B C B A, or part of our office team, this training is for you. Over the next few minutes, we will talk about why ethics matters so much in our work, how to keep healthy professional boundaries with the families we serve, and what it means to stay within your role. We will also cover honest documentation and billing, conflicts of interest, respectful language, everyday professional habits, and what to do if something does not feel right. At the end, there is a short quiz. Let's get started.

slides.heading: Why Ethics Matters in ABA
bullets: Our clients are often young and vulnerable
We work inside homes, schools and the community
Families trust us with their child and their privacy
One bad choice can harm a client and our practice
slides.narration: Most of our clients are children with autism, and many of them cannot easily tell someone if something goes wrong. Their parents trust us to come into their homes, their schools, and their daily lives. That is a lot of trust. Ethics is simply how we protect that trust. It means putting the client's well-being first, being honest, and acting the same way whether or not anyone is watching. When we make good choices, kids make progress and families feel safe. When someone makes a poor choice, it can hurt a child, damage a family's trust, and put the whole practice at risk. Good ethics is not just about avoiding trouble. It is part of doing great therapy.

slides.heading: The Ethics Codes That Guide Us
bullets: R B T Ethics Code 2.0 applies to all RBTs
BCBAs follow the BACB Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts
Codes are set by the BACB, which certifies us
Spectrum Squad's policies add to these codes
slides.narration: Our field has written ethics codes, and they are not optional. The B A C B, which is the Behavior Analyst Certification Board, is the organization that certifies R B Ts and B C B As. If you are an R B T, you are expected to follow the R B T Ethics Code, version two point zero. B C B As follow the B A C B's Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts. These codes cover things like honesty, client dignity, confidentiality, boundaries, and working within your competence. Your certification depends on following them. On top of these codes, Spectrum Squad has its own policies. If you are ever unsure what a code or policy means in a real situation, ask your supervisor. Asking is always the right move.

slides.heading: Boundaries in Clients' Homes
bullets: You are a professional guest, not a family friend
Gifts: follow Spectrum Squad's policy, ask first
Politely decline meals; keep the focus on the client
No rides in your car unless policy allows it
slides.narration: Working in a family's home can feel very personal. Parents may offer you dinner, invite you to a birthday party, or hand you a gift card for the holidays. These offers usually come from a kind place, but you are there as a professional, not as a family friend. When it comes to gifts, follow Spectrum Squad's policy, and check with your supervisor before accepting anything. A simple, friendly response works well, like, thank you so much, that is really kind, but I need to check our policy first. It is also best to politely decline meals and keep your attention on the session. And do not give clients or family members rides in your personal car unless Spectrum Squad's policy specifically allows it and your supervisor has approved it.

slides.heading: Dual Relationships
bullets: Only one role with a client family: their provider
No babysitting, nannying or side jobs for families
No dating or business deals with family members
If you already know a family, tell your supervisor
slides.narration: A dual relationship, also called a multiple relationship, happens when you have more than one role with a client or their family. Here is a very common example. A mom loves how you work with her son, and she asks if you could babysit on Saturday nights for some extra cash. It might seem harmless, but now you are both her child's therapist and her paid babysitter. That mixes things up, makes it harder to stay objective, and can confuse the child. The answer is a kind but clear no. The same goes for side jobs, dating a family member, or going into business with a family. And if you are assigned to a family you already know, like a neighbor or someone from your church, tell your supervisor right away so they can decide what is best.

slides.heading: Social Media and Personal Info
bullets: Do not friend or follow client families online
Never post client photos, names or stories
Keep your personal phone number private
Use Spectrum Squad's approved ways to communicate
slides.narration: Social media is another place where boundaries can blur fast. Do not send or accept friend requests or follows from client families, even if they ask first. You can say something like, I really appreciate that, but our policy is that we do not connect with families on social media. Never post photos, names, videos, or stories about clients, even without a name and even if it is a sweet moment. Someone could still figure out who it is. Also, keep your personal phone number and personal details private. When families need to reach you about scheduling or sessions, use the communication methods Spectrum Squad has approved. This protects the family's privacy and your own.

slides.heading: Stay Within Your Scope
bullets: RBTs work under the supervision of a BCBA
Never change a program or plan on your own
No diagnoses or clinical advice to parents
Refer clinical questions to the BCBA
slides.narration: Scope of competence means only doing the work you are trained and authorized to do. R B Ts always work under the supervision of a B C B A. You carry out the treatment plan, collect data, and share what you see. You do not change goals, programs, or procedures on your own, even if you think something would work better. Instead, bring your idea to your B C B A. Parents will often ask you questions like, do you think he has A D H D too, or should we stop his medication? It can feel helpful to answer, but you should not give a diagnosis or clinical advice. A great response is, that is a really good question, let me make sure your B C B A follows up with you. Then actually pass it along.

slides.heading: Honest Documentation and Billing
bullets: Session notes must show what really happened
Never bill for time you did not work
Record actual start and end times
Complete and verify notes on time
slides.narration: Your session notes and data are legal records, and they are used for billing insurance. They must reflect what actually happened. If a session started late, ended early, or a program was not run, write that down honestly. Never round up your time, copy and paste an old note, or write about things you did not do. Never bill for time you did not work, and never sign or verify a session that did not happen the way it was recorded. Here is an example. A session gets cut short by thirty minutes because the family had an emergency. The right thing is to document the real end time, even if that means fewer billable hours. Billing for time not worked can be insurance fraud, and it can lead to serious legal trouble. Also, finish and verify your notes on time, following Spectrum Squad's policy.

slides.heading: Conflicts of Interest
bullets: Your choices should never serve personal gain
Don't sell products or services to client families
Don't recruit families away to other providers
When in doubt, disclose it to your supervisor
slides.narration: A conflict of interest happens when your personal interests could get in the way of doing what is best for the client. For example, selling skin care products or essential oils to a client's parent, recommending a friend's tutoring business, or encouraging a family to follow you to another agency. Even if you mean well, these situations can pressure families and cloud your judgment. Families should never feel that their child's care is tied to buying something or doing you a favor. If you are not sure whether something counts as a conflict, the safest step is to tell your supervisor and let them help you decide. Being open about it protects everyone.

slides.heading: Dignity and Respectful Language
bullets: Treat every client with dignity and respect
Describe behavior, not labels like bad or naughty
Never talk about clients in front of others
Respect each family's culture and choices
slides.narration: Every client deserves to be treated with dignity. That means how we act and how we talk. Describe behavior in clear, neutral terms. Instead of saying he was being bad today, say he hit the table three times when asked to clean up. Avoid labels, jokes, or nicknames that could be hurtful. Never talk about a client's behavior in front of other people, or in front of the client as if they are not there. Many of our clients understand much more than they can say. Respect each family's culture, values, and choices, even when they are different from your own. And remember, conversations about clients are private, so keep them to the people who need to know.

slides.heading: Everyday Professionalism
bullets: Be on time; give notice for cancellations
Phone away during sessions unless used for work
Dress per Spectrum Squad's dress code
Follow the same standards at school and in public
slides.narration: Professionalism shows up in small, everyday habits. Be on time for every session. If you are running late or need to cancel, let your supervisor and the office know as early as possible, following Spectrum Squad's cancellation policy. Frequent late arrivals and last minute cancellations disrupt a child's progress and a family's day. During sessions, keep your personal phone put away unless you are using it for work, like collecting data. Texting or scrolling while a client is in your care is not okay, and it can also be a safety issue. Dress in a way that is clean, practical, and follows Spectrum Squad's dress code. These same standards apply whether you are in a home, a school, the clinic, or out in the community.

slides.heading: Reporting Concerns & Consequences
bullets: Speak up to your supervisor, BCBA or the owner
The BACB also accepts reports of ethics violations
Report concerns in good faith; ask if unsure
Violations can mean discipline or loss of credential
slides.narration: If you see something that seems unethical, or if you make a mistake yourself, speak up. Start with your supervisor or your B C B A. If you are not comfortable with that, or the concern involves them, you can go to the owner of Spectrum Squad. The B A C B also has a process for reporting ethics concerns about certified people, and certificants have their own duty to self-report certain things to the B A C B. Reporting a concern honestly and in good faith is the right thing to do. Keep in mind that suspected child abuse or neglect has its own legal reporting rules, which are covered in separate training. Ethics violations can have real consequences, including retraining, discipline, losing your job, action against your certification by the B A C B, and in cases like billing fraud, legal penalties.

slides.heading: Recap and Quiz
bullets: Stay professional: one role, clear boundaries
Stay in scope and refer clinical questions
Document and bill only what really happened
Take the quiz; you need 80% to pass
slides.narration: Great job. Let's quickly review. Ethics in A B A is about protecting the trust families place in us. Follow the ethics codes and Spectrum Squad's policies. Keep clear boundaries, which means checking policy before accepting gifts, no babysitting or side jobs for families, and no connecting on social media. Stay within your scope and send clinical questions to the B C B A. Write honest notes and only bill for time you actually worked. Avoid conflicts of interest, use respectful language, and be on time and present during sessions. If something feels wrong, speak up. Now it is time to take the quiz. You will need a score of eighty percent or higher to pass. Good luck.

quiz.question: A parent asks you, the RBT, to babysit their child on weekends for extra money. What should you do?
choices: Accept, since it is outside of work hours
Accept, but only if you are paid in cash
Kindly decline because it creates a dual relationship
Accept and tell your supervisor afterward
quiz.explanation: Babysitting for a client family gives you a second role with them, which is a dual relationship. Politely decline.

quiz.question: A client's mom sends you a friend request on social media after a great session. What is the best response?
choices: Politely decline and explain the policy is not to connect with families
Accept it but hide your posts from her
Accept since she sent the request first
Ignore it and post a photo of the session instead
quiz.explanation: Staff should not friend or follow client families on social media, even if the family asks first.

quiz.question: During a session, a parent asks you whether her son might also have ADHD. As an RBT, what should you say?
choices: Tell her yes, based on what you have seen
Tell her no so she does not worry
Suggest she change his medication
Say it is a good question and make sure the BCBA follows up
quiz.explanation: RBTs should not give diagnoses or clinical advice. Refer clinical questions to the BCBA and pass them along.

quiz.question: A session scheduled for two hours ended 30 minutes early because of a family emergency. How should you document it?
choices: Record the full two hours since it was not your fault
Record the actual end time, even though billable time is less
Make up the time by adding it to next week's note
Leave the note blank
quiz.explanation: Session notes must reflect what actually happened. Billing for time not worked can be insurance fraud.

quiz.question: You think a different reinforcer would work better for a client's program. What should you do?
choices: Bring your idea to your BCBA
Change the program yourself and see if it works
Ask the parent to approve the change
Change it, then update the data sheet
quiz.explanation: RBTs work under BCBA supervision and do not change programs on their own. Share ideas with the BCBA.

quiz.question: A family offers you a holiday gift card. What is the best first step?
choices: Accept it, since refusing could seem rude
Accept it and keep it secret
Thank them and check Spectrum Squad's policy with your supervisor
Ask for a larger gift instead
quiz.explanation: Follow Spectrum Squad's gift policy and check with your supervisor before accepting anything.

quiz.question: You sell skin care products on the side. Is it okay to offer them to client parents?
choices: Yes, if you give them a discount
Yes, as long as you do it after sessions
Yes, if the parents seem interested
No, it is a conflict of interest and can pressure families
quiz.explanation: Selling products to client families mixes personal gain with client care, which is a conflict of interest.

quiz.question: Which is the most respectful way to describe a client's behavior in a session note?
choices: He was being bad and naughty today
He was a nightmare during cleanup
He hit the table three times when asked to clean up
He acted like a typical autistic kid
quiz.explanation: Describe behavior in clear, neutral terms and avoid hurtful labels to protect the client's dignity.

quiz.question: You notice a coworker regularly writes notes for sessions that ended early as if they ran the full time. What should you do?
choices: Ignore it because it is not your business
Report your concern to your supervisor, BCBA or the owner
Post about it on social media
Start doing the same so it looks consistent
quiz.explanation: Speak up about ethical concerns in good faith. Start with your supervisor or BCBA, or go to the owner.

quiz.question: During a home session, your phone keeps buzzing with personal texts. What is the professional choice?
choices: Keep your phone away and use it only for work tasks like data collection
Reply quickly while the client plays
Let the parent watch the client while you text
Take a personal call in the next room
quiz.explanation: Personal phone use during sessions is distracting and can be a safety issue. Use your phone only for work.
